lead: Paul says that faith comes by hearing, and asks whether the word has really reached the whole world. Jesus says that the word heard has to reach the heart, down to the anger we keep inside and the brother we have not forgiven. Today's saint, St John of Damascus, adds that since the Word became flesh, the eye too may receive him in holy icons.

r.h: Faith comes from what is heard
set: Paul is still answering the question of Romans 9–11: why have so many in Israel not yet accepted Jesus as Messiah? He rules out the idea that they had no chance to hear. He writes with sorrow and love for his own people (9:1–3), and he goes on to declare that God has not rejected them (11:1). Chapters 9–11 must be read together; a verse taken alone can easily mislead.
str: v. 17: the principle: faith comes from hearing, and hearing from the word of Christ.
v. 18: have they not heard? Psalm 19:4.
vv. 19–20: did Israel not understand? Deuteronomy 32:21 and Isaiah 65:1.
kw: The word means both the act of hearing and the message heard. Christian faith is not an idea we think up; it comes to us from outside.
This can mean the word that comes from Christ or the word about Christ (as the POC takes it). Some later manuscripts read “the word of God”.
From Deuteronomy 32:21. In 11:11–14 Paul explains the aim: the faith of the nations is meant to stir Israel to come closer, not to replace it.
vv: So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.
The preaching of the Church is more than information. Christ himself speaks through it.
for “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

Psalm 19 speaks of the heavens telling God's glory without words. Paul applies the verse to the preachers of the Gospel. He means the word has gone out far and wide, not that every individual has already heard.
“I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.”
God takes the first step. The nations who were not looking for him are Paul's example, and all of us who did nothing to earn the Gospel stand among them.
ch: St Paul VI quotes v. 17 to show that preaching by word remains necessary in every age (Evangelii Nuntiandi 42). St John of Damascus, whom the Church remembers today, shows how the same Gospel can also reach us through the eye. The Catechism quotes his teaching that the God who had no body has now become visible in the flesh, so that we may make an image of what we have seen of God (CCC 1159), and adds that image and word illuminate each other (CCC 1160).

set: This is the first of the six sayings in Matthew 5 that begin “You have heard”. Jesus has just said that he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it (5:17). So he does not weaken “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13); he takes it down to its root in the heart. The word “council” in v. 22 refers to the Sanhedrin, the high court.
str: vv. 21–22: from murder to anger and insult, with rising penalties.
vv. 23–24: at the altar: go first and be reconciled.
vv. 25–26: on the road to court: settle while there is time.
kw: From the Hebrew gê hinnōm, the valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31). It became an image for final ruin.

An insult that denies a person's worth. The word before it in the Greek is the Aramaic raka, “empty-head”, which the NRSV renders “if you insult”. Contempt treats a person as nothing, and it is murder begun in the mind.
A very small Roman coin (quadrans). “The last penny” means the debt will be paid in full.
vv: So when you are offering your gift at the altar, if you remember that your brother or sister has something against you,
Note who has the grievance. It is not “if you are angry with someone”, but if someone has something against you. Then you take the first step.
leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.
In the Temple this was a startling picture. Worship stops for the sake of reconciliation. Worship itself is not cancelled: “then come and offer”.
Truly I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny.
A warning given while there is still time. The picture is of debts left unsettled until it is too late.
ch: The Catechism says that in recalling this commandment the Lord adds the prohibition of anger, hatred and vengeance (CCC 2262, 2302), and that from the Sermon on the Mount onward he insists on reconciliation with one's brother before presenting an offering at the altar (CCC 2608). The Didache, a very early Christian manual, already applies these words to the Eucharist: no one at odds with a companion should join the gathering until reconciled, so that the sacrifice may not be defiled (in substance, Didache 14).

qa: No. Jesus himself looked at people “with anger” at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5), and Paul writes, “Be angry but do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). The passion of anger is not sinful in itself. It becomes sin when we consent to the wish to harm, when we feed it and hold on to it (CCC 1767; 2302).
rite: Before the great thanksgiving of the anaphora, the Holy Qurbono has the sign of peace passed from the altar to the people. Matthew 5:23–24 is the Gospel behind that moment. In this fast, today's reading asks each of us to ask: who has something against me, and what will I do about it before Yaldo? St John of Damascus, a monk of the Lavra of St Sabbas near Jerusalem, is honoured in East and West; he gives a reason for the icons before which Eastern Christians pray.
study: Faith comes from what is heard. How much time do I give to hearing the word of Christ during this fast?
Is there anyone who has something against me? What first step can I take before I next go to the Holy Qurbono?
